I don't have any XR devices so can't seem to run the MRP, but a function that can probably help you is:
https://docs.godotengine.org/en/3.6/tutorials/physics/interpolation/advanced_physics_interpolation.html#get-global-transform-interpolated

Regarding the PR, you can do physics interpolation either client (scene) side or on the server. Sometimes we do it on the client side and sometimes server side.

Client side is often easier to implement (and indeed the mechanism is already built in to help do this via `get_global_transform_interpolated()`, although care has to be taken over priming). This function is primarily for users, but can also be used by core. Although having said that, in `Cameras` we do this manually as it gets around priming issues - it depends whether the node will always be active or will be switched on and off.

`Cameras` is a good example to see how they do it if you want to try client side, probably the 3D camera as it is slightly simpler. You may want to use `NOTIFICATION_INTERNAL_PROCESS` and `NOTIFICATION_INTERNAL_PHYSICS_PROCESS`.

The reason for doing it server side is, in most cases, for efficiency. So for e.g. large number of canvas items, or 3d nodes, we do the interpolation on the server, because it potentially is more efficient by e.g. avoiding lots of calls to `set_transform()` across the command queue on every frame, and is especially more efficient when the frame rate is higher than the tick rate.

On the other hand for single special items that there are only one or two of in a scene at once (e.g. `Cameras`) we do sometimes do the interpolation client side, as there is no significant loss to efficiency, and it keeps the server side code as simple as possible (indeed the overall code complexity is less).

I suspect for your XR origin it may be less complex to do the interpolation client side, and keep the server updated each frame. But doing it server side as in the PR isn't necessarily "wrong", it's just worth considering that you can do it the other way around. Ultimately it's up to the XR maintainers which way they prefer (and in some cases it only works sensibly one way around).

For targets on the client side you will also often want to use `get_global_transform_interpolated()` so you get a predicted interpolated position, instead of the physics tick position. This is the technique used for IK, where IK targets are evaluated each frame.

My initial approach was actually calling `set_process_internal` and updating the transform of the `XRServer` on each render frame with the interpolated value, basically what you just said of doing it in the client side. However, after taking a look at other implementations I thought It would be more appreciated to keep it similar to those as they seemed more performant than *forcing* an update every frame. I completely missed  `Camera3D::_update_camera` 😅
I agree that doing it similar to what the camera does is better here as it will be way easier to maintain and should work perfectly fine. We can only have 1 `XROrigin3D` node active at a time so only 1 would be processing internally, meaning the performance gain of doing it on the server side would be unnoticeable.

Try this for `fake_hand.gd`:
```
extends Node3D

var offset = Vector3()

# Called when the node enters the scene tree for the first time.
func _ready() -> void:
	DisplayServer.mouse_set_mode(DisplayServer.MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED)
	physics_interpolation_mode = Node.PHYSICS_INTERPOLATION_MODE_OFF
	pass # Replace with function body.


# Called every frame. 'delta' is the elapsed time since the previous frame.
func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	var tr = get_parent().get_global_transform_interpolated()
	tr.origin += offset
	global_transform = tr

var mouse_sensitivity = 0.002
func _input(event):
	if event is InputEventMouseMotion and Input.mouse_mode == Input.MOUSE_MODE_CAPTURED:
		offset.x += event.relative.x * mouse_sensitivity
		offset.y += -event.relative.y * mouse_sensitivity
```

EDIT: The approach I was trying didn't quite work when moving the parent, I was setting the global transform directly in `XRNode3D::_pose_changed`. If instead the we save the pose transform and apply it as an offset to the parent interpolated transform on every internal process it works fine:

```cpp
Node3D *parent = Object::cast_to<Node3D>(get_parent());

if (parent && parent->is_physics_interpolated_and_enabled() && !is_set_as_top_level()) {
	set_global_transform(parent->get_global_transform_interpolated() * pose_offset);
}
```

Another issue I found is if a `MeshInstance3D` is the child of one of those nodes, you will get the following warning from time to time: `Non-interpolated instance triggered from physics process` this is caused because `VisualInstance3D` seems to call `RenderingServer::instance_set_transform` on `NOTIFICATION_TRANSFORM_CHANGED` but that notification is received on physics frame by `SceneTree::flush_transform_notifications` in `SceneTree::physics_process`. You are correct, in that it's not as problematic as changing interpoated nodes outside of physics process, but I still decided in the general case it was worth warning (for now):

1) Physics interpolation warnings only kick off with repeated use, so changing a few initial transforms is no problem. It identifies a regular pattern of use.
2) The regular changing of transforms on physics ticks is indicative of common user misunderstanding how to use physics interpolation among beginners.
3) Even with additional transforms sent per frame, sending transforms on physics ticks is superfluous and will reduce performance 

Regarding (2), the general paradigm for physics interpolation is:
* Interpolation ON for a node - move on physics tick
* Interpolation OFF for a node - move on frame

It is only now we are starting to deal with these special cases (IK, ragdoll, XR) that we may have to address this problem that you mention of propagating transforms on physics ticks. It's possible that there will be a simple fix in some way preventing the propagation (but as you say watching for special circumstances where it is desired).

The alternative would be to identify these circumstances and turn off the warning, but that still leaves (3) and is susceptible to the worst kind of problem, that the user *thinks* everything is working correctly, but they are moving non-interpolated nodes on physics tick only. Ideally we want it to be *obvious* when the user is doing something wrong.

Ah no, it's something far more obvious: You've placed a physics node (`AnimatableBody3D`) on a non-interpolated branch of the scene tree. You've set `FakeHand` to OFF.

This unsurprisingly won't work well.

In fact going from non-interpolated branch to an interpolated sub branch is likely to go horribly wrong, it's really not supported (or envisaged), maybe I should add a warning for this. I'm not sure there is a use-case, but if you can think of one let me know.
